title: The Angel of the LORD
lead: A heavenly messenger who speaks for God and sometimes as God, from Hagar's spring to the call of Gideon and the birth of Samson. Readers have taken him as an angel who bears God's name, as a visible form of God himself, or, in much Christian reading, as the Son before his birth.

sections.h: Who is the angel of the LORD?
sections.b:
The Hebrew mal'akh YHWH means "messenger of the LORD." In several stories the line between the messenger and God blurs. The angel speaks to Hagar, and she gives a name to "the LORD who had spoken to her" (Genesis 16:7–13). At the burning bush "the angel of the LORD" appears, but "God" calls from the bush (Exodus 3:2–6). In Judges the angel speaks in the first person of bringing Israel out of Egypt (Judges 2:1), and with Gideon the text moves between "the angel of the LORD" and "the LORD" (Judges 6:11–24). Manoah fears death because "we have seen God" (Judges 13:22).

There are three main readings. Many Jewish interpreters and many modern scholars hold that he is a created messenger who speaks in God's name, as an envoy speaks for his king. Others think the figure is a way to speak of God appearing in visible form while keeping God above the world; some critical scholars think "angel of" was added in places by later scribes to soften a direct meeting with God. From Justin Martyr on, many Christian writers saw the angel as the Son of God appearing before the incarnation, a "Christophany." The text does not settle the question.
